monitored_text: Resources / Machining Design / Wire Harness Assembly Wire Harness Assembly Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 23 min read Published November 26, 2026 Wire harness assembly is the process of cutting, stripping, crimping, connecting, and bundling wires into one shaped, tested assembly that connects the electrical parts of a machine or vehicle. Wire harness assembly turns loose wires into one organized unit that installs in a single step. A wire harness assembly (cable harness assembly, electrical harness assembly) is the finished harness made of wires, terminals, connectors, and protective covering. Operators build the unit on a harness board from a drawing, then test the unit before shipment. Vehicles, robots, and factory machines rely on the finished harness to carry power and signals. Clear steps, tools, and tests set the quality of wire harness assembly. Engineers and buyers need to know the assembly steps, the board and tools, and the tests that check each harness. Molded and extruded parts (connector housings, seals, sleeving) go into the harness, whereas brackets and enclosures support the finished unit. Custom and industrial orders start with a drawing, a bill of materials, and quantities. Standards (IPC/WHMA-A-620) define acceptance criteria for crimps, routing, and labeling. What Is Wire Harness Assembly? Wire harness assembly is the process of turning loose wires into one organized assembly. Operators cut wires to length, strip the ends, fit terminals, and place the terminals in connector housings. Bundling on a board, covering, and testing follow the connector step. The harness then installs in one piece instead of wire by wire. The term names the finished product too, so a wire harness assembly is a process and a part. Harness makers use the shorter word harnessing for the same work. A drawing sets wire gauge, color, length, and connector positions, which keeps each unit identical. Machines handle repeat steps (cutting, stripping, crimping), whereas hands handle routing and taping. Supplier catalogs list the work under cable harnessing. Automotive, industrial, medical, and aerospace builders order the assemblies for power and signal circuits. Quality checks confirm that each circuit matches the drawing before shipment. How Does a Wire Harness Assembly Differ From a Cable Assembly? A wire harness assembly differs from a cable assembly in how the wires are held. A wire harness ties separate insulated wires together with tape, sleeving, or conduit. A cable assembly places the wires inside one outer jacket. Harnesses are lighter and cost less, since the wires need no shared jacket. Cable assemblies resist harsh environments (oil, moisture, abrasion) and carry shielding better. A bundle that includes jacketed cable runs is called a cable harness assembly. Shielding blocks electrical noise from motors and drives. Wire harnesses suit fixed routes in vehicles and control panels, whereas cable assemblies suit moving joints and outdoor runs. Cable assemblies cost more per meter, since jackets and shields add material. Suppliers build the two types, so the combined product carries the name wire harness and cable assembly. The drawing lists the exact construction, which removes doubt before production. Weight, cost, and environment decide the choice. Is a Cable Harness the Same as a Wire Harness? Yes, a cable harness is mostly the same as a wire harness in everyday use. The two terms name an organized bundle of wires, terminals, and connectors. A cable harness means a harness that includes jacketed cables, whereas a wire harness means bundled single wires. Jacketed cables (shielded pairs, coaxial lines, multi conductor cable) carry data or sensor signals. Shielded cable adds cost and stiffness, which affects routing and bend radius. Suppliers apply the terms loosely, so one quote for a cable harness lists wire runs, jacketed cable, or a mix. The drawing settles the question, since the wire list shows each conductor type. Buyers check the drawing before ordering to confirm shielding, jacket material, and connector style. A mismatch in terms causes wrong quotes and delays. Matching part numbers and wire specifications remove the confusion. How Do Assembly Services Support Wire Harness Assembly? Assembly services support wire harness assembly by combining parts from multiple processes into one finished unit. A harness goes into a larger product (control cabinet, engine bay, robot arm). The provider gathers molded housings, machined pins, extruded sleeving, and fabricated brackets. Technicians fit the parts to the harness, then check fit against the drawing. One supplier handling the full build cuts handoffs and shortens lead time. Kitting delivers matched part sets to the line, which prevents wrong part mix ups. Sub assemblies (harness plus bracket, harness plus junction box) arrive ready to install. Final testing covers the harness in the finished unit, which catches fit and routing errors. Each unit moves from kitting to testing under one quality record. Labels, packaging, and documents match the customer’s line schedule. Builders that need a harness alongside supporting parts gain one point of contact through assembly services . Can a Wire Harness Assembly Be Outsourced to a Manufacturing Partner? Yes, a wire harness assembly can be outsourced to a manufacturing partner. Companies outsource harness assembly to a specialist since the work needs trained operators, crimp tools, and testing equipment. A harness shop keeps crimp applicators, harness boards, and continuity testers ready. The buyer sends a drawing, a bill of materials, and quantities for a quote. Target dates, labeling needs, and test requirements round out the request. The supplier reviews the package and flags routing or sourcing risks. A first article sample confirms fit before production starts. Outsourcing converts fixed equipment and labor costs into a per unit price. Buyers audit quality certifications (ISO 9001, IPC/WHMA-A-620) before award. Small teams gain access to skills that take years to build in house. Clear drawings and revision control keep the partner and the buyer aligned. What Process Do Manufacturers Follow for Wire Harness Assembly? Manufacturers follow eight steps for wire harness assembly, from drawing review to final packing. Each step builds on the last, which makes order the core of the wire harness assembly process. To know the process manufacturers follow for wire harness assembly, follow the eight steps listed below. Review the drawing and the bill of materials . The drawing lists wire gauges, colors, lengths, and connector positions. The bill of materials names the wire, terminals, connectors, and sleeving. Engineers flag missing parts before cutting begins. Cut the wires to length and strip the ends . A wire cutter or cutting machine trims each wire to the drawing length. A stripper removes insulation from the ends at the set strip length. Clean strands prevent weak crimps. Crimp the terminals and check the crimp . A crimping tool or press fixes each terminal onto the stripped end. Operators check crimp height and tug each terminal to confirm grip. A bad crimp is scrapped and redone. Insert the terminals into the connector housings . Each terminal pushes into its numbered cavity until the lock clicks. A pin chart prevents swapped positions. A light pull confirms the terminal is seated. Lay the wires on the harness assembly board . The board holds a full size drawing with pegs that set routes and branch lengths. Operators follow the drawing from connector to connector. Consistent layout keeps each harness identical. Bundle the wires and add labels . Tape, cable ties, sleeving, or conduit hold the wires together. A heat gun shrinks heat shrink tubing over splices and connector backs. Labels carry part numbers and circuit marks. Add clips, grommets, and overmolded boots . The drawing marks the positions of clips, grommets, and boots. Clips fix the routing on the vehicle or machine. Boots give strain relief and block dust at connector exits. Test and inspect the harness, then pack it . A multimeter or test board checks continuity against the netlist. Inspectors confirm color, length, labels, and connector fit. Tested harnesses ship in labeled bags or trays. How Is a Wire Harness Assembly Board Used? A wire harness assembly board is a flat board that holds a full size drawing of the harness. Pegs or nests on the board hold the wires and connectors in the right route and length. Operators lay each wire along the printed path, so each harness comes out the same. Connector holders grip the housings at the correct angle, which frees the hands for insertion. Branch points sit at marked positions, which keeps lengths within tolerance. Accurate layout starts with a well made wire harness assembly board. Boards come in wood, plastic, or aluminum, depending on the duty cycle. Wood boards cost little, whereas aluminum boards hold flatness and resist wear. Teams make or order a custom board and fixtures for each harness. Tilting or rotating boards give access to long harnesses. Color coded pegs and wire lists guide placement from the drawing. Operators verify the layout with a ruler or a gauge before the first build. Can CNC Machining Make a Wire Harness Assembly Board? Yes, CNC machining can make a wire harness assembly board. Plastic or aluminum boards, nests, and pegs are cut to the drawing, which gives accurate, repeatable layouts. Machines hold positions near plus or minus 0.1 millimeters, which keeps branch lengths consistent. Pockets in the board hold connector housings at the exact angle. Peg holes and slots follow the digital file, so a revised drawing needs only a new program. Plastic sheet (acetal, HDPE) machines quickly and resists wear. Aluminum plate (6061) stays flat and resists wear for long production runs. Engraved part numbers and wire labels print directly into the surface. Machined boards suit repeat orders, since the same program remakes a worn board. Tight tolerances and clean edges protect operators and wires during routing. Precision boards and nests for harness work come from CNC machining . Does 3D Printing Make Wire Harness Assembly Jigs Faster? Yes, 3D printing makes wire harness assembly jigs faster for low volume work. Printers produce custom jigs, nests, and cable guides in days without tooling. Revisions need only an edited file, which helps when the harness layout changes. Fused deposition modeling (FDM) prints low cost holders from PLA or PETG. Selective laser sintering (SLS) makes tough nylon PA12 nests that resist wear. Printed connector holders match the exact housing shape. Cable guides keep bend radius above the minimum for the wire. Printed parts cost little per piece at low quantities. Layer lines and softer material limit life under heavy daily use. Hot work areas near heat guns soften plastic jigs. Aluminum or machined boards suit long runs. Engineers test the fit on a real harness before ordering a machined board. Prototype builds and pilot runs suit 3D printing best. When Is Manual Wire Harness Assembly Better Than Automation? Manual wire harness assembly is better than automation for low volumes, varied harness types, and complex routing or connectors. Skilled operators adapt to new wire lists without machine reprogramming. Automation is better for high volumes of simple cut, strip, and crimp work. Wire processing machines handle thousands of terminals per shift with consistent crimp height. Setup time limits automation on short runs, since each part number needs new applicators and programs. Flexible wires lack stiffness, so robots struggle to grip and seat them in connectors. Harnesses in production use machines and hand work together. Machines prepare the wires, whereas operators route, tape, and insert. Complex harnesses (dozens of branches, mixed connectors) stay manual from board to tape. Volume forecasts and variant counts guide the choice. Hybrid lines add automatic taping and ultrasonic splicing where the product is simple. Quality systems check crimp force on each path. Is Wire Harness Assembly Still Done by Hand? Yes, wire harness assembly is still done by hand for routing, taping, and connector work. Wires are flexible, so robots struggle to hold and place them. Harness layouts vary from one order to the next, which limits fixed automation. Machines handle cutting, stripping, and crimping at high speed. Operators insert terminals into housings and feel the lock click. Hands lay wires on the board, wrap tape, and fit clips and grommets. Trained operators spot routing errors that machines miss. Automated lines feed prepared wires to the board, yet people complete the assembly. Ultrasonic splicing and automatic taping reduce manual steps on simple products. Complex harnesses with dozens of branches need the greatest share of hand work. Fully automatic harness lines remain rare. Inline sensors on crimp presses lower scrap and rework. Labor skill remains a core part of harness quality. How Is a Wire Harness Assembly Tested? A wire harness assembly is tested against the drawing before the harness ships. Inspectors start with a visual check of wire, color, length, and connector type. A continuity test finds opens and shorts by checking each circuit against the netlist. A pull test on sample crimps confirms that terminals hold on the wire. Higher voltage harnesses get an insulation resistance or high voltage test. Standards (IPC/WHMA-A-620) define the acceptance criteria for crimps, routing, and labeling. Class 2 suits standard industrial products, whereas Class 3 suits high reliability products. Test boards with mating connectors hold the harness and run a check in seconds. Failed units return for rework, then repeat the full test. Records or labels show that each harness passed testing. Traceability links the harness to a lot number and test result. Early detection of crimp and pinout errors prevents field failures. What Tests Check a Wire Harness Assembly for Defects? The tests that check a wire harness assembly for defects include continuity, short and open circuit, hipot, pull, and visual checks. Each test targets a different failure, from wrong pins to weak crimps. IPC/WHMA-A-620 and customer drawings define the acceptance limits. The tests that check a wire harness assembly for defects are listed below. Continuity Test : A continuity test confirms that each wire connects to the right pin. The tester compares the harness to the netlist from the drawing. Swapped or missing connections show up as failures. Short and Open Circuit Test : An open circuit test finds broken wires and unseated terminals. A short circuit test finds unwanted contact from wire to wire. The two checks run in seconds on a test board. Hipot or Insulation Resistance Test : A hipot test applies high voltage to confirm that insulation holds. An insulation resistance test measures leakage from conductor to conductor at 500 volts DC. Nicked insulation and moisture show up as low readings. Pull or Crimp Test : A pull test measures the force needed to extract a crimped terminal. Customer specifications set minimum force by wire size, in newtons. Weak crimps fail before the harness reaches the vehicle. Visual Inspection : Inspectors check strip length, wire color, labels, and connector fit. Crimp shape, strand capture, and sleeving position get a close look. Visual checks catch errors that electrical tests miss. Is Continuity Testing Enough for a Wire Harness Assembly? No, continuity testing is not enough for a wire harness assembly. Continuity testing shows that wires connect to the right pins. The test does not prove that a crimp is strong. The test does not prove that insulation handles voltage. A weak crimp passes continuity on the bench, then fails under vibration. Pull tests measure the force that holds each terminal on the wire. Insulation tests find nicked insulation, moisture, and contamination. Visual inspection confirms strip length, wire color, labels, and connector fit. Higher voltage harnesses need a hipot test at the voltage the drawing sets. Sample crimps get microsection checks (cross section analysis) for strand capture. The full set of checks protects the finished machine or vehicle. Continuity remains the first step, since the test flags opens, shorts, and swapped pins. What Parts Go Into a Wire Harness Assembly Besides Wire? A wire harness assembly uses parts besides wire, namely terminals, connector housings, seals, sleeving or conduit, tape, clips, grommets, labels, and brackets or enclosures. Terminals form the electrical joint on each wire end. Connector housings hold the terminals in numbered cavities. Seals keep water and dust out of the connector. Sleeving, conduit, and tape protect the bundle from abrasion and heat. Clips and grommets fix the routing and protect wires at panel holes. Labels carry part numbers and circuit marks. Wire gauge sets the terminal size, which keeps the crimp strong. Molding, extrusion, and fabrication make the supporting parts. Molded housings, seals, and clips come from injection molding. Extruded conduit and tubing come from plastic extrusion. Brackets and junction boxes come from sheet metal or molded plastic. Each part carries a rating for current, temperature, and sealing. Matching ratings across parts keep the assembly reliable. How Is a Wire Harness Assembly Connector Molded? A wire harness assembly connector is molded by injecting melted plastic into a steel mold. Housings and clips come from plastics (nylon 66, PBT), whereas seals come from silicone or rubber. Glass filled nylon 66 (PA66) melts near 260 degrees Celsius and holds strength under load. PBT absorbs less moisture and keeps dimensions stable. Flame retardant grades meet UL 94 V0 ratings. The mold shapes terminal cavities, locking latches, and seal grooves in one shot. Multi cavity steel tools make thousands of identical housings. Processors dry nylon pellets before molding to prevent voids and splay marks. Prototypes and short runs are made without full production tooling. Soft aluminum molds and printed molds cut cost for small batches. Engineers test fit and latch strength on the samples before steel tools are cut. Assemblers then add seals, terminal position assurance (TPA) locks, and connector position assurance (CPA) latches. Is Prototype Injection Molding Used for Wire Harness Connectors? Yes, prototype injection molding is used for wire harness connectors. The process makes small batches of connector housings or clips for fit and function tests. Engineers run the tests before production tooling is built. Aluminum tools cost less than hardened steel tools and are ready in weeks. Real production resins (nylon 66, PBT) show true strength, heat resistance, and shrinkage. Printed parts match the shape but not the material behavior. Housings from the tool confirm terminal fit, latch force, and seal compression. Samples reveal draft, wall thickness, and gate issues before steel is cut. Quantities from 50 to 500 parts cover validation builds. Test results feed the final drawing for production molds. Early molded samples reduce launch risk for new connector styles. Short run connector samples that match production resins come from prototype injection molding . Can Custom Overmolding Seal a Wire Harness Assembly? Yes, custom overmolding can seal a wire harness assembly. A molded boot over the connector and wire joint gives strain relief. The boot improves the seal against dust and moisture. A full waterproof rating depends on the part geometry, the materials, and ingress testing (IP67, IP68). Molten polymer (TPE, TPU, PVC, polyamide) flows around the joint and bonds to the cable jacket. Low pressure molding with polyamide hot melt suits delicate electronics. Injection overmolding with TPE or PVC suits volume runs. The molded body replaces loose boots and heat shrink at the cable exit. Material choice sets flexibility, temperature range, and chemical resistance. Bad bonding to the jacket leaves leak paths along the wire. Overmolded cable exits resist bending fatigue better than loose boots. Sealed and rugged harnesses gain strain relief and protection through custom overmolding . What Protective Sleeving is Used in a Wire Harness Assembly? A wire harness assembly uses sleeving, conduit, tape, and heat shrink to protect the bundle from abrasion, heat, and fluids. Braided polyethylene terephthalate (PET) sleeving expands over bundles and suits tight bends. Split loom (polyethylene, nylon) wraps finished bundles, whereas closed conduit slides on before crimping. Corrugated nylon conduit resists abrasion, oil, and engine heat. Cloth tape and PVC tape bind bundles at low cost. Heat shrink tubing seals splices and connector backs, and adhesive lined versions block moisture. Temperature rating comes first, since PVC suits 80 degrees Celsius and silicone suits 200 degrees Celsius. Flexibility matters at door hinges and robot joints, where stiff conduit cracks. Environment sets the rest, from oil and fuel to UV and salt spray. Flame retardant grades meet UL 94 V0, and halogen free grades limit smoke. The drawing names the sleeving type, size, and color for each branch. A wrong size slips off or squeezes the wires. Is Plastic Extrusion Used to Make Wire Harness Sleeving? Yes, plastic extrusion is used to make wire harness sleeving. The process pushes melted plastic through a die to form a continuous profile. Conduit, tubing, and wire insulation come from the process. Pellets of PVC, nylon, polypropylene, or polyethylene melt in a heated barrel. A screw pushes the melt through the die, and a water bath cools the profile. Corrugated tubing forms when the profile passes through a vacuum mold with ridges. Wire insulation is extruded over stranded copper conductors in the same way. Split loom is slit in line as the tube leaves the die. Controlled wall thickness and consistent diameter keep products uniform. Material choice sets abrasion, chemical, and flame resistance. Long continuous lengths are cut to size for each harness. Protective conduit and tubing for harnesses are produced in volume through plastic extrusion . How Do Brackets and Enclosures Support a Wire Harness Assembly? Brackets and enclosures support a wire harness assembly by holding the harness in place and protecting connectors. Brackets fix the harness at set points, which prevents sagging and chafing against edges. Clamps hold wires along frames, panels, and engine parts. Junction boxes house splices, fuses, and relays away from dust and water. Guards cover the bundle near moving parts and sharp edges. Heat shields deflect radiant heat from exhaust and motors. Parts are made from sheet metal or molded plastic. Sheet metal suits strength, heat resistance, and shielding. Molded plastic suits low weight, low cost, and electrical insulation. Material choice follows the operating temperature and exposure. Rubber isolators on brackets absorb vibration before the vibration reaches the wires. Brackets follow the harness drawing, so clip positions match the routing. Accurate hole positions keep clips aligned during installation. Corrosion resistant finishes (zinc plating, powder coating) extend service life. Is Sheet Metal Fabrication Used for Wire Harness Brackets? Yes, sheet metal fabrication is used for wire harness brackets. Formed sheet metal brackets and clips route and support harnesses in vehicles and equipment. Laser cutters trim flat blanks from a digital file. Press brakes bend the blanks into brackets, clip mounts, and guards. Punching adds clip holes and mounting slots. Common materials include galvanized steel, 304 stainless steel, and 5052 aluminum from 0.8 to three millimeters thick. Deburred edges and rolled flanges prevent insulation cuts. Zinc plating or powder coating resists corrosion. Revised brackets need no new die, since cutting follows the digital file. Prototype brackets ship in days, which suits fit checks on a vehicle. Volume runs move to stamping dies for lower cost per part. Bracket makers form the parts to the harness drawing through sheet metal fabrication . What Custom Wire Harness Assembly Options Are Available? Custom wire harness assembly options include choices of wire type and gauge, connectors, length, sleeving, labels, and testing. The buyer drawing, sample, or specification defines each custom wire harness assembly . Wire type covers PVC, XLPE, silicone, and PTFE insulation, with gauges chosen for current load. Connector choice sets pin count, sealing, and mating style. Length tolerances and branch positions follow the drawing. Sleeving, tape, and labels match the environment and the customer marking rules. Testing options range from continuity checks to hipot and pull tests. The buyer orders by sending the drawing, the bill of materials, and the quantities. Three routes exist: build in house, buy from a harness maker, or copy an existing harness. Copying starts from a sample, which suppliers measure and document. Buying from a harness maker gives access to trained operators, tooling, and test equipment. Building in house suits teams with low volumes and skilled staff. How Do You Order a Custom Wire Harness Assembly? You order a custom wire harness assembly by preparing a drawing and bill of materials, requesting quotes, and approving a first article. The drawing lists wire gauges, colors, lengths, pin assignments, and branch layout. The bill of materials names connector part numbers, terminals, seals, and sleeving. Quantities, annual volume, and target dates guide the quote. Applicable standards (IPC/WHMA-A-620, UL 758) and test requirements go on the request. A supplier needs wire type, connector part numbers, lengths, labels, and test requirements to quote. Suppliers return quotes with tooling cost, unit price, and lead time. A first article or prototype confirms fit, routing, and pin assignments on the real product. The buyer reviews the sample and sends revisions. Approval of the sample releases production. Revision control keeps the drawing and the build in step. Packaging and labeling needs round out the order details. Samples and drawings together shorten the quote cycle. Can Rapid Prototyping Test a Wire Harness Assembly Design? Yes, rapid prototyping can test a wire harness assembly design. The method makes quick samples of the housings, brackets, and fixtures around a harness. Engineers check fit on the vehicle or machine before production. 3D printed connector covers show clearance, latch reach, and seal fit. Laser cut brackets confirm routing and clip positions in days. Machined pins and test fixtures confirm contact fit. Technicians hand crimp a sample harness and adjust branch lengths after each trial. Revisions cost little, since no steel mold or stamping die exists yet. Each trial updates the drawing, which locks the final layout. Five to 20 sample harnesses cover typical fit trials. Short lead times keep the schedule on track. Validated samples move to production tooling and first article approval. Quick turn samples of surrounding parts and fixtures come from rapid prototyping . Where Is an Industrial Wire Harness Assembly Used? An industrial wire harness assembly is used in factory machines, robots, control panels, and heavy equipment. Factory machines (conveyors, CNC machines, packaging lines) need harnesses that resist oil and coolant. Robots need flex rated cable that survives millions of bends. Control panels need color coded conductors and numbered ferrules for field service. Heavy equipment (excavators, cranes, tractors) needs sealed connectors and tough sleeving. Vibration, oil, dust, and heat set the material and sealing choices. Builders order each automotive wire harness assembly to a drawing that matches the duty cycle. Harnesses for moving axes use fine stranded copper and soft PUR jackets. Voltage ranges from 24 volts DC for control to 480 volts AC for motors. Washdown areas need IP67 or IP69K connectors. Compliance rules (UL 758, NFPA 79, IEC 60204) guide machinery wiring. Power plants, renewable energy systems, and trucks use the same approach. Is Wire Harness Assembly Used in Automotive Manufacturing? Yes, wire harness assembly is used in cars. Each vehicle carries multiple harnesses (engine, dashboard, body, door, lighting). One of the largest uses of the process is automotive wire harness assembly . A passenger car carries a harness network that links the battery, engine control module, sensors, lighting, and controls. Circuits run at 12 volts in cars, 24 volts in trucks, and 48 volts in mild hybrids. Insulation (PVC, XLPE, silicone) matches the heat zone. Standards (ISO 6722, SAE J1128) set the wire requirements. IATF 16949 certification signals automotive quality management. Production uses automatic cutting and crimping, followed by manual routing on boards. Each harness gets a continuity test before shipment. Weight and routing matter, since the harness must fit narrow body spaces. Electric vehicles add high-voltage cables and shielded lines. Cars, trucks, and buses depend on the automotive wire harness . Disclaimer The content appearing on this webpage is for informational purposes only. Accurate layout starts with a well made wire harness assembly board. Boards come in wood, plastic, or aluminum, depending on the duty cycle. Wood boards cost little, whereas aluminum boards hold flatness and resist wear. Teams make or order a custom board and fixtures for each harness. Tilting or rotating boards give access to long harnesses. Color coded pegs and wire lists guide placement from the drawing. Operators verify the layout with a ruler or a gauge before the first build. Can CNC Machining Make a Wire Harness Assembly Board? Yes, CNC machining can make a wire harness assembly board. Plastic or aluminum boards, nests, and pegs are cut to the drawing, which gives accurate, repeatable layouts. Machines...

sections.heading: When Is Manual Wire Harness Assembly Better Than Automation?
sections.text: When Is Manual Wire Harness Assembly Better Than Automation? Manual wire harness assembly is better than automation for low volumes, varied harness types, and complex routing or connectors. Skilled operators adapt to new wire lists without machine reprogramming. Automation is better for high volumes of simple cut, strip, and crimp work. Wire processing machines handle thousands of terminals per shift with consistent crimp height. Setup time limits automation on short runs, since each part number needs new applicators and programs. Flexible wires lack stiffness, so robots struggle to grip and seat them in connectors. Harnesses in production use machines and hand work together. Machines prepare the wires, whereas operators route, tape, and insert. Complex harnesses (dozens of branches, mixed connectors) stay manual from board to tape. Volume forecasts and variant counts guide the choice. Hybrid lines add automatic taping and ultrasonic splicing where the product is simple. Quality systems check crimp force on each path. Is Wire Harness Assembly Still Done by Hand? Yes, wire harness assembly is still done by hand for routing, taping, and connector work. Wires are flexible, so robots...

sections.heading: How Is a Wire Harness Assembly Tested?
sections.text: How Is a Wire Harness Assembly Tested? A wire harness assembly is tested against the drawing before the harness ships. Inspectors start with a visual check of wire, color, length, and connector type. A continuity test finds opens and shorts by checking each circuit against the netlist. A pull test on sample crimps confirms that terminals hold on the wire. Higher voltage harnesses get an insulation resistance or high voltage test. Standards (IPC/WHMA-A-620) define the acceptance criteria for crimps, routing, and labeling. Class 2 suits standard industrial products, whereas Class 3 suits high reliability products. Test boards with mating connectors hold the harness and run a check in seconds. Failed units return for rework, then repeat the full test. Records or labels show that each harness passed testing. Traceability links the harness to a lot number and test result. Early detection of crimp and pinout errors prevents field failures.

sections.heading: What Tests Check a Wire Harness Assembly for Defects?
sections.text: What Tests Check a Wire Harness Assembly for Defects? The tests that check a wire harness assembly for defects include continuity, short and open circuit, hipot, pull, and visual checks. Each test targets a different failure, from wrong pins to weak crimps. IPC/WHMA-A-620 and customer drawings define the acceptance limits. The tests that check a wire harness assembly for defects are listed below. Continuity Test : A continuity test confirms that each wire connects to the right pin. The tester compares the harness to the netlist from the drawing. Swapped or missing connections show up as failures. Short and Open Circuit Test : An open circuit test finds broken wires and unseated terminals. A short circuit test finds unwanted contact from wire to wire. The two checks run in seconds on a test board. Hipot or Insulation Resistance Test : A hipot test applies high voltage to confirm that insulation holds. An insulation resistance test measures leakage from conductor to conductor at 500 volts DC. Nicked insulation and moisture show up as low readings. Pull or Crimp Test : A pull test measures the force needed to extract a crimped terminal. Customer specifications set minimum force by wi...

sections.heading: What Parts Go Into a Wire Harness Assembly Besides Wire?
sections.text: What Parts Go Into a Wire Harness Assembly Besides Wire? A wire harness assembly uses parts besides wire, namely terminals, connector housings, seals, sleeving or conduit, tape, clips, grommets, labels, and brackets or enclosures. Terminals form the electrical joint on each wire end. Connector housings hold the terminals in numbered cavities. Seals keep water and dust out of the connector. Sleeving, conduit, and tape protect the bundle from abrasion and heat. Clips and grommets fix the routing and protect wires at panel holes. Labels carry part numbers and circuit marks. Wire gauge sets the terminal size, which keeps the crimp strong. Molding, extrusion, and fabrication make the supporting parts. Molded housings, seals, and clips come from injection molding. Extruded conduit and tubing come from plastic extrusion. Brackets and junction boxes come from sheet metal or molded plastic. Each part carries a rating for current, temperature, and sealing. Matching ratings across parts keep the assembly reliable.

sections.heading: How Is a Wire Harness Assembly Connector Molded?
sections.text: How Is a Wire Harness Assembly Connector Molded? A wire harness assembly connector is molded by injecting melted plastic into a steel mold. Housings and clips come from plastics (nylon 66, PBT), whereas seals come from silicone or rubber. Glass filled nylon 66 (PA66) melts near 260 degrees Celsius and holds strength under load. PBT absorbs less moisture and keeps dimensions stable. Flame retardant grades meet UL 94 V0 ratings. The mold shapes terminal cavities, locking latches, and seal grooves in one shot. Multi cavity steel tools make thousands of identical housings. Processors dry nylon pellets before molding to prevent voids and splay marks. Prototypes and short runs are made without full production tooling. Soft aluminum molds and printed molds cut cost for small batches. Engineers test fit and latch strength on the samples before steel tools are cut. Assemblers then add seals, terminal position assurance (TPA) locks, and connector position assurance (CPA) latches. Is Prototype Injection Molding Used for Wire Harness Connectors? Yes, prototype injection molding is used for wire harness connectors. The process makes small batches of connector housings or clips for fit and func...

sections.heading: What Protective Sleeving is Used in a Wire Harness Assembly?
sections.text: What Protective Sleeving is Used in a Wire Harness Assembly? A wire harness assembly uses sleeving, conduit, tape, and heat shrink to protect the bundle from abrasion, heat, and fluids. Braided polyethylene terephthalate (PET) sleeving expands over bundles and suits tight bends. Split loom (polyethylene, nylon) wraps finished bundles, whereas closed conduit slides on before crimping. Corrugated nylon conduit resists abrasion, oil, and engine heat. Cloth tape and PVC tape bind bundles at low cost. Heat shrink tubing seals splices and connector backs, and adhesive lined versions block moisture. Temperature rating comes first, since PVC suits 80 degrees Celsius and silicone suits 200 degrees Celsius. Flexibility matters at door hinges and robot joints, where stiff conduit cracks. Environment sets the rest, from oil and fuel to UV and salt spray. Flame retardant grades meet UL 94 V0, and halogen free grades limit smoke. The drawing names the sleeving type, size, and color for each branch. A wrong size slips off or squeezes the wires. Is Plastic Extrusion Used to Make Wire Harness Sleeving? Yes, plastic extrusion is used to make wire harness sleeving. The process pushes melted plastic...

sections.heading: How Do Brackets and Enclosures Support a Wire Harness Assembly?
sections.text: How Do Brackets and Enclosures Support a Wire Harness Assembly? Brackets and enclosures support a wire harness assembly by holding the harness in place and protecting connectors. Brackets fix the harness at set points, which prevents sagging and chafing against edges. Clamps hold wires along frames, panels, and engine parts. Junction boxes house splices, fuses, and relays away from dust and water. Guards cover the bundle near moving parts and sharp edges. Heat shields deflect radiant heat from exhaust and motors. Parts are made from sheet metal or molded plastic. Sheet metal suits strength, heat resistance, and shielding. Molded plastic suits low weight, low cost, and electrical insulation. Material choice follows the operating temperature and exposure. Rubber isolators on brackets absorb vibration before the vibration reaches the wires. Brackets follow the harness drawing, so clip positions match the routing. Accurate hole positions keep clips aligned during installation. Corrosion resistant finishes (zinc plating, powder coating) extend service life. Is Sheet Metal Fabrication Used for Wire Harness Brackets? Yes, sheet metal fabrication is used for wire harness brackets. Formed...

sections.heading: What Custom Wire Harness Assembly Options Are Available?
sections.text: What Custom Wire Harness Assembly Options Are Available? Custom wire harness assembly options include choices of wire type and gauge, connectors, length, sleeving, labels, and testing. The buyer drawing, sample, or specification defines each custom wire harness assembly . Wire type covers PVC, XLPE, silicone, and PTFE insulation, with gauges chosen for current load. Connector choice sets pin count, sealing, and mating style. Length tolerances and branch positions follow the drawing. Sleeving, tape, and labels match the environment and the customer marking rules. Testing options range from continuity checks to hipot and pull tests. The buyer orders by sending the drawing, the bill of materials, and the quantities. Three routes exist: build in house, buy from a harness maker, or copy an existing harness. Copying starts from a sample, which suppliers measure and document. Buying from a harness maker gives access to trained operators, tooling, and test equipment. Building in house suits teams with low volumes and skilled staff.

sections.heading: How Do You Order a Custom Wire Harness Assembly?
sections.text: How Do You Order a Custom Wire Harness Assembly? You order a custom wire harness assembly by preparing a drawing and bill of materials, requesting quotes, and approving a first article. The drawing lists wire gauges, colors, lengths, pin assignments, and branch layout. The bill of materials names connector part numbers, terminals, seals, and sleeving. Quantities, annual volume, and target dates guide the quote. Applicable standards (IPC/WHMA-A-620, UL 758) and test requirements go on the request. A supplier needs wire type, connector part numbers, lengths, labels, and test requirements to quote. Suppliers return quotes with tooling cost, unit price, and lead time. A first article or prototype confirms fit, routing, and pin assignments on the real product. The buyer reviews the sample and sends revisions. Approval of the sample releases production. Revision control keeps the drawing and the build in step. Packaging and labeling needs round out the order details. Samples and drawings together shorten the quote cycle. sections.heading: Where Is an Industrial Wire Harness Assembly Used?
sections.text: Where Is an Industrial Wire Harness Assembly Used? An industrial wire harness assembly is used in factory machines, robots, control panels, and heavy equipment. Factory machines (conveyors, CNC machines, packaging lines) need harnesses that resist oil and coolant. Robots need flex rated cable that survives millions of bends. Control panels need color coded conductors and numbered ferrules for field service. Heavy equipment (excavators, cranes, tractors) needs sealed connectors and tough sleeving. Vibration, oil, dust, and heat set the material and sealing choices. Builders order each automotive wire harness assembly to a drawing that matches the duty cycle. Harnesses for moving axes use fine stranded copper and soft PUR jackets. Voltage ranges from 24 volts DC for control to 480 volts AC for motors. Washdown areas need IP67 or IP69K connectors. Compliance rules (UL 758, NFPA 79, IEC 60204) guide machinery wiring. Power plants, renewable energy systems, and trucks use the same approach. Is Wire Harness Assembly Used in Automotive Manufacturing? Yes, wire harness assembly is used in cars. Each vehicle carries multiple harnesses (engine, dashboard, body, door, lighting). text_excerpt: Resources / Machining Design / Wire Harness Assembly Wire Harness Assembly Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 23 min read Published November 26, 2026 Wire harness assembly is the process of cutting, stripping, crimping, connecting, and bundling wires into one shaped, tested assembly that connects the electrical parts of a machine or vehicle. Wire harness assembly turns loose wires into one organized unit that installs in a single step. A wire harness assembly (cable harness assembly, electrical harness assembly) is the finished harness made of wires, terminals, connectors, and protective covering. Operators build the unit on a harness board from a drawing, then test the unit before shipment. Vehicles, robots, and factory machines rely on the finished harness to carry power and signals. Clear steps, tools, and tests set the quality of wire harness assembly. Engineers and buyers need to know the assembly steps, the board and tools, and the tests that check each harness. Molded and extruded parts (connector housings, seals, sleeving) go into the harness, whereas brackets and enclosures support the finished unit. Custom and industrial orders start with a drawing,...
